questions.question: Robert Paine pried every ochre sea star off a stretch of rocky shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, from 1963 on, and threw them far out into the bay; a stretch beside it he left alone. Fifteen species clung to the cleared rock at the start, and the sea stars there eat barnacles, mussels, limpets and chitons. What happened to the number of species on the cleared rock within a year?
questions.answer: It fell to 8, as the mussels crowded out the rest
choices: It fell to 8, as the mussels crowded out the rest
It fell to 8, as the limpets grazed the seaweeds away
It rose to 22, as the sea stars' prey were spared
It stayed at 15, as each species grew more plentiful
questions.context: Without the sea stars, barnacles spread over the rock, and then mussels, the strongest competitors for space, crowded out the seaweeds, limpets and chitons; the limpets and chitons left rather than multiplying, and only years later did the mussels come close to taking it all. By eating the mussels, the sea star had kept room for everyone else. Paine called such a species, whose loss changes its community far more than its numbers suggest, a keystone species, after the stone that locks an arch together.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4, NGSS MS-LS2-4) teaches how removing a predator ripples through a community; Paine's sea-star removal is the classic experiment, and it gave ecology the keystone species.

questions.question: Wolves had been gone from Yellowstone National Park for about 70 years when 31 wolves from Canada were set free there in 1995 and 1996. Over the next 15 years, young willows and aspens along some streams of the park's northern range began to grow taller. Ecologists who credit the wolves call it a trophic cascade. By their account, how did the wolves help the trees?
questions.answer: They thinned out the elk that browsed on the young shoots
choices: They thinned out the elk that browsed on the young shoots
They thinned out the beavers that felled the young trees
They thinned out the bison that trampled the streambanks
They thinned out the hares that gnawed the young bark
questions.context: Elk are the wolves' main prey, and the elk of the northern range fell from about 16,800 in 1995 to about 8,300 by 2004, so fewer were left to nibble young willow and aspen shoots; beavers, which need willow, rose from one colony to nine, and bison grew more plentiful. Ecologists still argue over how much was the wolves' doing: bears, human hunters, a hard winter and drought also cut the elk, beavers set free north of the park spread in, and measuring only the tallest young aspens made the comeback look bigger than it was.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches the trophic cascade, a top predator's removal or return rippling down through its prey to the plants; Yellowstone's wolves are the textbook case, taught with its open debate.

questions.question: Killer whales began hunting sea otters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands in the 1990s, as the seals and sea lions they usually eat grew scarce. Along the open coast otter numbers fell by about a quarter each year, while in a lagoon the whales could not enter, they held steady. Over the same years the kelp forests of the open coast thinned to about a twelfth of their old density. What linked the whales to the kelp?
questions.answer: Urchins, freed from the otters, grazed it down
choices: Urchins, freed from the otters, grazed it down
Fish, freed from the seals and sea lions, grazed it down
Seal droppings, grown scarce, no longer fed it
Whales, chasing otters through it, broke it apart
questions.context: Sea otters eat sea urchins, and with the otters gone the urchins boomed, rising about eightfold, and grazed the kelp down. Four levels were linked, whale to otter to urchin to kelp, so a change at the top flipped the bottom: more hunting by the whales meant less kelp. James Estes, who led the study, was sure the whales were to blame partly because the otters of Clam Lagoon, out of the whales' reach, did not decline.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches predicting how a crash at one level ripples through several others; the otter, urchin and kelp chain is a standard middle-school cascade, and the killer whales add a fourth level.

questions.question: Cane toads, brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat beetles in the sugar cane, have spread across northern Australia, and glands in their skin hold a poison that kills many native animals that try to eat them. Ecologists studied a river valley in the Kimberley for years before and after the toads arrived. Crimson finches there neither eat the toads nor are eaten by them. What happened to the finches?
questions.answer: More of their chicks lived, as nest-raiding lizards died off
choices: More of their chicks lived, as nest-raiding lizards died off
Fewer of their chicks lived, as the toads ate their insects
Fewer of their chicks lived, as toad poison fouled the water
Nothing changed, as the finches and the toads never met
questions.context: Monitor lizards, which raid the finches' nests for eggs and chicks, died from eating the toads: the water monitors fell by close to half over five years, and the finches' fledging success, a measure of how many young lived to leave the nest, rose from 55 to 81 percent. An invader that few native animals can safely eat can thus help one native species by killing its predator, two links away. The toads, meanwhile, never did control the cane beetles.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches how an invasive species with no natural predators ripples through a food web; the cane toad is the standard Australian example.

questions.question: Wild rabbits, set loose in Australia for hunting in 1859, spread across much of the continent. In its deserts, feral cats and foxes feed heavily on rabbits but also hunt native hopping mice. From 1995 a new rabbit virus cut the rabbits of South Australia's deserts sharply. What happened to the hopping mice over the following years?
questions.answer: They spread widely, as the cats and foxes grew fewer
choices: They spread widely, as the cats and foxes grew fewer
They grew scarce, as the cats and foxes hunted them more
They grew scarce, as the virus spread to them as well
They stayed the same, as the rabbits never ate them
questions.context: Four kinds of small native mammals, two hopping mice among them, came to cover far more of the desert than before, most of them several times as much. Ecologists credited both ends of the web: the rabbits no longer ate the native mammals' food, and the cats and foxes that lived on rabbits grew fewer with them. The virus infects only European rabbits, so it never touched the mice.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches how invasive species and their removal ripple through a food web; rabbits in Australia are the classic invasive example.

questions.question: Zebra mussels, carried to North America in ships' ballast water, appeared in New York's Hudson River in 1991. Within two years billions of them lived on the riverbed, straining floating algae from the water, and the algae fell by four-fifths. Shad and herring of the open river then grew fewer and grew more slowly. What linked the mussels to these fish?
questions.answer: The tiny animals that the fish feed on
choices: The tiny animals that the fish feed on
The water plants that grow along the riverbed
The sunfish that share the river with them
The bigger fish that hunt them in open water
questions.context: The floating algae feed zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, and zooplankton feed the young of open-water fish; with the algae strained out, small zooplankton nearly vanished and the larger kinds fell by about half, so the fish went short. The mussels never touched the fish: the harm climbed the food web from its base. The clearer water suited sunfish of the shallows, which grew more plentiful, while the river's native mussels, once over a billion, began to disappear.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches how an invasive species ripples through the transfer of energy in a food web; zebra mussels are a standard American example.

questions.question: Ecologists set hot fires and cool fires on patches of savanna in northern Australia and left other patches unburned. They trapped two kinds of native rodent on every patch and fitted 38 pale field rats with radio collars. Both kinds grew fewer after the fires, and fewest after the hot ones. What did the study find had cut their numbers?
questions.answer: More of them were caught by predators
choices: More of them were caught by predators
More of them starved, with their food burned
More of them moved off to unburned ground
More of them died in the flames and smoke
questions.context: The team found no sign that the fires themselves killed the rodents, starved them, stopped their breeding or drove them away; instead more of them were eaten, most of all where hot fires had stripped away the grass that hid them, and the team found rats killed by feral cats and by snakes. Feral cats in the region walk up to 12 kilometres to hunt on fresh burns, and their filmed hunts in open ground ended in a kill 70 percent of the time against 17 percent in dense grass or among rocks. A fire's harm does not end with the flames: it passes on through the predators, so the researchers urge cooler, patchier burns.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches how a natural disaster such as a fire ripples through a food web; here the ripple runs through the predators, as a field experiment showed.

questions.question: Rinderpest, a cattle disease that also kills wildebeest, kept the wildebeest of the Serengeti few until it was wiped out there in the 1960s. The herds then grew from about a quarter of a million to more than a million by the late 1970s. Over the same years the number of trees in the Serengeti changed too. How did it change, and why?
questions.answer: It rose, as fewer fires swept the grazed grass
choices: It rose, as fewer fires swept the grazed grass
It fell, as the herds ate more of the young trees
It fell, as the herds trampled more of the seedlings
It stayed the same, as the herds ate only grass
questions.context: Grazed short by over a million mouths, the grass left too little fuel for the fires that had swept the plains, and fire tends to kill small trees. With fewer fires, young trees grew up, and Tony Sinclair, who watched it happen, judged there had not been so many trees since the 1800s. Ricardo Holdo's team weighed other causes, such as elephants and rainfall, and found that the fall in fire explained the trees best.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches how a population boom ripples through a food web; the Serengeti's wildebeest show it reaching the trees through fire.

questions.question: George Woodwell's team measured the insecticide DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) along a food chain in a Long Island estuary in the 1960s. The plankton held about 0.04 parts per million, small fish 0.5, larger fish 2, and fish-eating birds such as ospreys about 25. What makes the level climb at each step up the chain?
questions.answer: Each eater stores the DDT from its many meals
choices: Each eater stores the DDT from its many meals
Each bigger animal has more body to hold the DDT
Each bigger animal is hit by more of the spray
The DDT multiplies inside each animal's body
questions.context: DDT dissolves in fat but hardly at all in water, and bodies break it down only slowly, so an animal stores most of what it swallows instead of passing it out. A fish eats a great many plankton and an osprey a great many fish, so each stores the DDT of countless meals, and by these numbers the level climbs more than six hundred times from plankton to bird; ecologists call it biomagnification. Parts per million measure the DDT in each kilogram of body, so size alone cannot explain the climb, and Rachel Carson warned of just this building-up in Silent Spring in 1962.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches pollution rippling through a food web; DDT building up from plankton to fish-eating birds is the standard example of biomagnification.

questions.question: Derek Ratcliffe kept finding broken eggs in the nests of peregrine falcons in Britain in the 1950s. He weighed and measured peregrine eggshells kept in museums and private collections, some laid more than a century before, and compared them with eggs from his own surveys. What did the shells show?
questions.answer: Steady for a century, then a sudden drop
choices: Steady for a century, then a sudden drop
Thinner and thinner, little by little, for a century
No thinner than before, so the parents were to blame
Thin in some years and thick in others, with no pattern
questions.context: Ratcliffe's measure of shell thickness held steady for over 125 years, then dropped by about a sixth from 1947, soon after farmers in Europe and America began spraying DDT on a large scale, and shells so thin cracked as the parents brooded them. The drop came so fast that the chemical industry argued it was too quick to be DDT's doing, but David Peakall later found enough DDE, a breakdown product of DDT, in British eggs of 1946 to thin them, and Joseph Hickey and Daniel Anderson found the same thinning in the United States from 1947, in ospreys and bald eagles among others. After the United States banned DDT in 1972 the birds came back: helped also by protection from shooting, bald eagle nesting pairs in the lower 48 states rose from 417 in 1963 to 9,789 by 2007.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L4) teaches pollution rippling through a food web; DDT thinning the eggshells of eagles, ospreys and falcons, found by measuring old museum eggs, is its best-known result.

fa96b4fd9f.why: Judge (medium): the key and 'It fell to 1, as the mussels covered all the rock' differed only by the count, so a number decided it. That choice is gone; in its place is 'It fell to 8, as the limpets grazed the seaweeds away', the T1 cascade a student expects (predator gone, grazer booms, plants fall), which is wrong here: the limpets and chitons left the cleared rock (F2, F32). The two 'fell to 8' choices are now decided by the ecology. The stem now lists the sea star's prey as barnacles, mussels, limpets and chitons (F32), so the limpet choice stays live. Fact (low): 'within a year' is kept; the fact-check found it in SciAm, Scitable and Grokipedia. The context now says the limpets and chitons left rather than multiplying.

2593fea18f.why: Judge (low, clarity): 'They cut the elk' could read as 'wounded'; all four choices now say 'thinned out'. Stem, key fact and context unchanged.

5d81c07557.why: Judge (medium, overlap): with 'Sea otters eat sea urchins' in the stem the question was the T1 one-step chain. The stem now gives the kelp's fall (to a twelfth, F11) and asks what linked the whales to the kelp, so the student must know the otter-urchin link himself. Choices: the urchins (key), a rival cascade in the same shape (fish freed from the seals and sea lions; wrong, the urchins grazed it, F11), fewer seal droppings to feed it and whales breaking it (both wrong; the urchins, up eightfold, grazed it down, F11). An 'otters tore it up' choice was not used, since the stem's falling otter numbers rule it out. Fact-check (error): the context now says 'more hunting by the whales meant less kelp', not 'more whales'.

a93f48b7c3.why: Fact-check (error): 'An invader with no natural enemies' overclaimed (keelback snakes eat toads unharmed and meat ants kill young ones, F34); the context now says 'An invader that few native animals can safely eat'. Stem and choices unchanged.

3e5c758fab.why: Fact-check (error): 'several times as much' was not true of the spinifex hopping mouse (F17); the context now says 'far more of the desert than before, most of them several times as much'. Stem and choices unchanged.

f1671ec4e6.why: Judge (high): 'ground freshly burned by an intense fire' is open ground, so the stem handed over the key 'open country'; the key was also one predator's hunting by habitat (lane, low). Re-keyed on the ripple itself, from the same research group's fire experiment (Leahy, Legge, McGregor and others, F31): rodents grew fewer after fires, and of five tested causes only predation was supported. The four choices are four of those tested causes (predation, starvation, leaving, the flames), so common sense cannot rule any out and the stem names no predator. McGregor's GPS trips and filmed hunts (F20, F21) move to the context as the why.

7fd439d92c.why: Fact-check (uncertain): the water figure (3 parts per trillion) is Time's 1969 popular number, not the paper's; it is dropped from the stem, and the context's 'more than eight million times from water to bird' is now 'more than six hundred times from plankton to bird' (0.04 to 25, F26). Judge (low, voice): the spelled-out name stays, because the acronym gate requires it. Choices and key unchanged.

11870f3841.why: Judge (medium): the key and 'Steady for a century, then thinner from 1939 on' differed only by a year, so date recall decided it. The choices now key the shape of the record, the evidence that pointed to a new cause: steady for over 125 years, then a sudden drop from 1947 (F28; so quick that the chemical industry argued it came too soon after DDT's arrival, F33). Wrong: a slow century-long thinning, no thinning with the parents to blame (the rival reading of the broken eggs, F28), and no pattern. The context keeps 1947 and DDT's spread; the 1939 aside is gone.
